A deliberate strategy

Sticking with my figure of 65.3%, it represents a significant increase over the full-year 2017 equivalent figure of 50%. Back then, main cabin revenue was 1.7 times Delta's premium cabin revenue, but as you can see above, Delta's premium cabin revenue exceeded main cabin revenue in the second quarter.

It's all part of a deliberate strategy to diversify Delta's revenue away from the extreme cyclicality of main cabin ticket revenue. As Esposito noted on the recent earnings call: "We're not growing Main Cabin seats. This is a multiyear, several years in a row, that we haven't grown this cabin. We won't be growing it next year either."

Moreover, Delta continues to grow its highly successful loyalty-related revenue alongside remuneration from co-branded credit cards with American Express (management expects to grow 10% to $9 billion in 2026). This is high-quality revenue, as SkyMiles is paid for up front and is less tied to flying volume.

Higher-quality earnings

While Delta is never really going to escape cyclical exposure, that exposure is a lot less than many investors think. Trading at just 12.4 times 2026 earnings estimates, the stock looks like an excellent value, with plenty of revenue streams (premium, loyalty, credit cards, etc.) that hold up well in a slowdown.

All told, Delta is improving the quality of its earnings, including its resilience during a slowdown. That's good news for investors.

text:
Melbourne has just made history, hosting Australia’s first-ever NFL regular season game. More than 100,000 game-day tickets sold almost instantly, the seventh largest attendance in NFL history. Fifty thousand international and interstate fans travelled for a three-day NFL festival, and 40 million more fans watched from around the world. It was a Super Bowl-sized experience, right here in Australia.

For the NFL, every game creates thousands of opportunities to connect with fans. As the league expands internationally, that opportunity is creating a parallel challenge for its marketing and creative teams. Fans expect content that is immediate and tailored to their country, their language, and even the team they may already have an affinity with.

Meeting that content demand is no longer simply a matter of producing more. It requires a different operating model for creating, managing, approving, personalising and distributing content at scale.

The NFL is working with Adobe to build an AI-powered content supply chain that connects creation, approvals, data, personalisation and distribution, helping content move more efficiently from an idea to a fan experience.

This season, the NFL has a record nine international games across four continents as its global audience continues to grow. To illustrate the scale, a single Sunday tune-in campaign designed to tell fans when, where and how to watch games across television, streaming, digital, social and international channels, can begin with about 6000 assets. That can expand to more than 89,000 assets across 15 languages, and more than 356,000 once adapted across different experiences.

Work of that magnitude once required extensive manual production. Today Adobe technology is helping the league, and its 32 clubs, orchestrate those variations more efficiently and respond at the speed fans expect.

Powered by Adobe CX Enterprise, the system brings together applications, AI and workflows spanning content creation, audience intelligence, journey orchestration and analytics. The NFL says the approach has reduced some content production times from days to minutes and, in certain cases, seconds.

Each of the NFL’s 32 clubs has its own fanbase, identity, commercial priorities, creative approach, sponsors and intellectual property. Many of the teams are international brands in their own right. As a result, the league needs a system that allows individual clubs autonomy while maintaining consistency and control across the wider organisation.

“Scale is everything for our marketing teams,” says Chi Ogbuehi, vice president, marketing technology and consumer products at the NFL. “From the way we create campaigns to the way we personalise experiences with AI, our marketers need a content supply chain that can grow and evolve with their expanding fanbase.”

One example is the NFL’s AI Template Assistant. Using Adobe’s brand-safe AI, it enables designers to convert approved Photoshop creative into automation-ready templates that can be reused across campaigns.

By connecting templates with NFL data and applying metadata and governance rules, the system can prepare assets for production at scale. According to the NFL, a process that previously took three to five weeks of manual creative production can now be completed in about 15 minutes.

Rather than choosing between quality and volume, teams can create more variations around the clubs, players and moments that matter to individual fans.

“The tug of war between speed and quality held our marketers back from owning content creation,” says Cole Feldman, senior product manager at the NFL.

He says AI-powered tools have enabled teams to produce and personalise brand-safe assets faster while expanding creative possibilities.

The result is a content engine designed not only for greater volume but for greater relevance, helping marketers respond to the rhythms of the season and the individual interests of fans across a rapidly expanding global audience, without sacrificing speed, quality, and brand control.

The NFL has also developed an AI Campaign Assistant that extends automation into campaign activation. Marketers can generate high volumes of production-ready content from a single approved creative source without requiring design or developer expertise.

The system supports a range of experiences that fans engage with each week, from game-day content and weekly programming to player polls and pre-game team comparisons. NFL schedules, match-up details, team information and player statistics can be pulled automatically into approved templates, while metadata rules determine which players, teams and supporting assets should appear in each piece of content.

During major broadcast events such as the annual NFL Draft, workflows can connect directly with league data and automatically incorporate draft selections, player imagery and other real-time information into creative assets.

Content that once took three hours to assemble can now be produced in four to five minutes. That means a newly drafted player can appear in content wearing his new team colours while fan attention and excitement are still peaking.

The broader lesson extends beyond sport.

As organisations pursue AI, the competitive advantage won’t come from generating more content, it will come from redesigning the systems around it. Automation becomes more valuable when it is connected to trusted data, approved creative, clear governance and workflows that people can actually use.

For the NFL, that foundation is increasingly important as international growth creates demand for more localised experiences. The league plans to expand multilingual content production during the 2026–2027 season.

When an NFL game in Melbourne can reach 40 million viewers and generate more than 340 million social media impressions, the content supply chain has to move at the speed of fan engagement.

name: Delta Airlines
title: Budget airline king Bill Franke warms to first-class seats and premium upgrades - CNBC
description:
The ultra-low-cost airline model that Franke, who goes by Bill, pioneered has faced a reckoning in recent years.
But since then, larger, more powerful rivals like United Airlines and Delta Air Lines have copied the model for their cheapest tickets.
His legacy stretches across the airline industry: Many top airline executives, including the CEOs of United Airlines and American Airlines , worked under him earlier in their careers.
Franke also ran Spirit Airlines until 2013, before becoming the chairman at Frontier at the end of that year.
Isom told CNBC in an interview in late June that Franke is "pretty good at giving jabs."
text:
SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. — For decades, William Augustus Franke, Frontier Airlines ' chairman and a serial airline investor, made a killing selling cheap plane tickets and charging fees to check bags, to pick seats and for everything else. Now, he says first-class seats and other traveler comforts are in order — at least in the United States.

Frontier is planning to roll out first-class seats next year on its Airbus fleet. It's also joined a growing list of airlines adding SpaceX 's Starlink Wi-Fi on board as it seeks to return to steady profitability.

"We're not trying to have a Singapore Airlines first class," Franke, 89, told CNBC in late June at the model airplane-filled offices of Indigo Partners, the private equity firm he founded. "What we're trying to do is give the consumer an option," he said, calling it at once upscale and competitive.

The ultra-low-cost airline model that Franke, who goes by Bill, pioneered has faced a reckoning in recent years. A jump in pilot salaries, maintenance costs and operating expenses, along with a boom in premium travel, have hit long-profitable and fast-growing budget carriers. Maintaining strong growth and keeping costs low were sacrosanct for that sector for years.

Another pillar was not giving things away for free. At the 2017 Dubai Air Show, where he made a record Airbus aircraft order for the empire of airlines he invested in, Franke likened some consumers to teenagers and "spoiled brats," saying they expected to get low fares and what are now add-ons without paying for them, CNBC reported at the time.

"They had been flying with all the amenities for ever and ever and that's what they think they ought to get," Franke said at the time.

But since then, larger, more powerful rivals like United Airlines and Delta Air Lines have copied the model for their cheapest tickets. They've started offering bare-bones fare options and adding fees for everything else. This year, they even brought that pricing strategy to their first classes and plush, long-haul suites to increase revenue, stripping customers who choose that option of a free seat choice, among other restrictions.

Franke has owned, operated or invested in budget airlines around the world, from Chile to Hungary to the Philippines to the U.S. He was an early investor in European budget carrier Ryanair.

His legacy stretches across the airline industry: Many top airline executives, including the CEOs of United Airlines and American Airlines , worked under him earlier in their careers.

Franke also ran Spirit Airlines until 2013, before becoming the chairman at Frontier at the end of that year.

He tried to merge the two carriers in 2022 but Spirit shareholders voted for another offer, all cash, from JetBlue Airways . That deal fell apart after a federal court ruled it violated antitrust laws in January 2024.

Struggling on its own, Spirit collapsed in May, the biggest U.S. airline failure in decades, leaving Frontier as the largest discounter in the country.

Franke said he's far from out of the game and remains a major Frontier shareholder.

"We see startup ideas probably one a month," he said.

Franke started flying frequently when he was a little kid because his father worked for the State Department and was based in Paraguay.

He said a lot has changed since. "Consumers are much smarter today" than they used to be, armed with new data and tools like artificial intelligence that help them better compare fares and options, he noted.

"None of the airlines are quite sure what AI ... is going to do to your decision to book," he said.

But "price and schedule are still at the top," Franke added.

"For a lot of consumers, whether the ticket costs $200 or $125 is not going to be the decision-maker, but for a lot of people it is still," he continued. "Middle class, younger flyers, they still focus on price."

But the ultra-low-cost and low-fare model has struggled in the United States. It's based on keeping costs minimal and maintaining rapid growth, both of which have been more difficult since the pandemic. Higher fuel prices since the start of the Iran war have been an added challenge.

Spirit is the obvious casualty, with its CEO saying it "ran out of runway" after facing increasing challenges, but Frontier has only been profitable one year since 2019 and JetBlue hasn't been profitable since that year.

"We're not forecasting next year, but the airline is certainly on the right trajectory to return to sustainable profitability," Frontier CEO Jimmy Dempsey said on a July 29 earnings call. He became the carrier's chief executive in December, succeeding Barry Biffle who headed the airline for close to a decade.

Airlines, including Frontier, have been jacking up fares to cover costs. August airfares were up more than 23% over last year, according to federal data released Sept. 11.

Frontier isn't alone in wanting to add pricier and roomier seats. Allegiant Air recently announced it would add a first class to its currently single-cabin planes, and JetBlue Airways is adding a domestic first class. Meanwhile, larger competitors are growing their premium cabins.

Franke said the new upscale moves don't fit everywhere, and that efficiency remains key.

"In the U.S. market where you have mature large airlines — Delta, United, American — who are changing the interior of their aircraft on a regular basis, it could well be that a low-cost or a lower-cost airline, in order to properly compete, needs to make adjustments to its business model," he said. "That doesn't mean you have to do that in an emerging market like Hungary or Peru."

Franke's former employees told CNBC that they keep up with him regularly.

Isom told CNBC in an interview in late June that Franke is "pretty good at giving jabs." For many years, they would bet on college football, specifically, games between Stanford University, where Franke studied, and Notre Dame, where Isom studied.

"His rule was fast pay makes fast friends," Isom recalled, showing CNBC some of his winnings: Chilean pesos with Franke's business card attached by paperclip and, in another win by Isom, euro coins taped to a sheet of paper with "PAID IN FULL" written out by his former boss.

Kirby told CNBC at an industry conference in Rio de Janeiro in June that after The Wall Street Journal profiled him this spring, Franke told him it made him "throw up in his coffee when he opened his newspaper." Franke didn't comment on that, but said he recalled the exchange.

Even still, Kirby called Franke a mentor, and clarified that he was "a hard-ass mentor."

"All of us, our formative years were working for Bill, getting screamed at by Bill. ... He should take more credit for that," he said. (Franke said he didn't yell at him. "That's just not me.")

Franke was demanding, especially when it counted, his alumni said.

Steve Johnson, American Airlines vice chair and chief strategy officer, and another Franke America West alum, likened Franke to a second father.

Johnson was a partner from 2003 to 2009 at Indigo when it owned Spirit. During the summer 2008 fuel spike that saw prices hit more than $147 a barrel (more than $200 in today's dollars), Spirit was running out of money but had a portfolio of fuel hedges, a series of contracts that locks in future pricing.

He was about to head to a California-bound plane that summer when Franke called him about the fuel and told him to "sell it now," Johnson recalled. They did and generated about $30 million. Oil prices later crashed.

"It turned out to be just exactly what Spirit needed," Johnson said.

text:
Steven Kolb, the chief executive of the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA), has resigned after footage showed him physically restraining two animal rights activists during a confrontation at New York Fashion Week.

“After 20 years leading the CFDA, I have made the difficult decision to step down as CEO and president,” he said in a statement.

“I am enormously proud of what we have built together and believe this is the right moment for both me and the organisation to begin a new chapter.”

Mr Kolb was placed on leave on Tuesday pending an incident review following a confrontation at New York Fashion Week’s COS show on Sunday.

Be the first to know when news breaks. Download our new app.

In a video, Mr Kolb was seen trying to hold back two PETA protesters who attempted to disrupt the show in a demonstration against the use of wool by H&M Group, which owns COS.

Kolb pushed a protester named Mason Melito and covered his mouth. He also wrestled another protester to the ground, holding her down with his arms and leg while covering her mouth with his hand.

Speaking to The Guardian afterwards, Mr Melito called the incident scary and said Mr Kolb’s actions were “completely uncalled for”.

Taking to Instagram Stories shortly after the distressing incident, Mr Kolb issued an apology for his “inappropriate” actions.

“I am deeply sorry and hold myself accountable,” the fashion chief wrote to his followers.

Claiming the outburst was entirely “out of character”, he admitted there was simply “no justification for physically restraining another person”.

Shortly after the clash, PETA US released a statement calling for animal cruelty in the industry to be taken seriously.

“Today’s actions show how top people in fashion use violence to silence people who expose how sheep are … killed for scarfs and sweaters,” PETA founder Ingrid Newkirk said in the statement obtained by news.com.au.

“PETA is calling on H&M and COS to ban wool from its collections and is urging everyone to shop elsewhere until they do.”

The CFDA is a non-profit organisation that supports and promotes American designers and brands. It also coordinates the official New York Fashion Week calendar.

A statement from the CFDA board, which features designers like Ralph Lauren, Thom Browne, Tory Burch, and Michael Kors, praised Mr Kolb as a committed leader and relentless advocate for American fashion during his more than 20 years at CFDA, including 15 years as CEO.

“We respect Steven’s decision to step down and are grateful for his many years of leadership and service to the CFDA and our industry. He leaves the organisation well positioned, with a clear mission and a dedicated team, to carry out the important work ahead as we look to the future of American fashion.”

The group has yet to name a successor.

Last December, the CFDA proudly announced it was banning animal fur at New York Fashion Week, though the ban excluded wool and other products derived from shorn animal hair.

text:
Eli Lilly and CompanyView company profile has launched a Phase 2 study of vepugratinib ( search )Search drug in adults with certain early bladder and upper tract urothelial cancers, according to a newly posted ClinicalTrials registry entry. The trial, named FORAY, will assess how well the oral agent controls low grade, intermediate risk tumors that carry FGFR3 ( search )Search target changes, and will track safety over time in a setting where new targeted options are limited.

Mechanism and Rationale

Vepugratinib ( search )Search drug, also known as LY3866288View drug details, is an oral drug designed to block FGFR3 ( search )Search target, a signaling pathway linked to tumor growth in some bladder and upper tract cancers. The stated goal of treatment is to delay or prevent disease return.

The study population consists of adults with non-muscle invasive bladder and upper tract urothelial cancer ( search )Search disease whose tumors harbor FGFR3 ( search )Search target alterations. The focus on low grade, intermediate risk disease places the program in an early-stage setting rather than advanced or metastatic disease.

Trial Design

FORAY is an interventional trial that randomly assigns participants to different treatment groups running in parallel. It is open label, meaning both physicians and patients know they are receiving vepugratinib ( search )Search drug. The trial's main purpose is treatment rather than prevention or diagnosis.

The registry lists the study as not yet recruiting. First submission and the latest update both carry the date September 15, 2026, indicating a fresh entry to the ClinicalTrials registry. Primary and final completion dates have not yet been posted. Each patient may be followed for up to five years, which points to long-term outcome and safety tracking as part of the study's design.

Positioning in Lilly's Oncology Pipeline

The FORAY listing reflects Lilly's continued push into targeted oncology beyond its current portfolio. Positive results in FGFR3 ( search )Search target-altered bladder and upper tract cancers could support a future niche launch in a precision medicine setting, and would place the program alongside other FGFR-directed efforts in development. Any clinical readout and subsequent regulatory path remain several years away given the trial's not-yet-recruiting status and the absence of posted completion dates.

description:

Why ICON Is Being Delisted Upbit attributed the delisting to security incident risks surrounding ICON that were never resolved.
text:
S&P Global (SPGI) has agreed to acquire OpenZeppelin, the smart contract security firm whose open-source code library sits behind more than $37 trillion in transferred value, and will run the auditor as a standalone business unit under its own name.

Founded in 2015, OpenZeppelin pairs security assessments and secure development services for decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols and traditional financial institutions with OpenZeppelin Contracts, a free library of standard token and contract implementations that the vast majority of the largest stablecoins and tokenized funds are built on.

South Korea’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Upbit, will end trading support for ICON’s ICX token by delisting the ICX/KRW pair on October 19, 2026. The exchange confirmed the move in a trading-support termination notice, completing a review that began in late August when ICX was first designated an investment caution asset over unresolved security risks. The decision removes the token’s main won-denominated market and gives holders a fixed window to exit before support ends.

Delisting Timeline and Mechanics

Trading for ICX against the Korean won will stop at 3:00 p.m. Korea Standard Time on October 19, and all outstanding orders will be cancelled once support ends. Upbit also said it will no longer process airdrops, wallet upgrades, migrations, or hard forks for the asset after the deadline, and holders must complete their withdrawals by November 18, 2026. The exchange urged users to settle any pending trades and move assets before those dates to avoid disruption. The sequence mirrors Upbit’s September decision to end trading support for Synthetix (SNX), another project it had flagged for review.

Why ICON Is Being Delisted

Upbit attributed the delisting to security incident risks surrounding ICON that were never resolved. The exchange placed ICX on an investment caution list in late August, a designation it uses to warn traders ahead of a potential delisting, and the token’s status was not lifted in the weeks that followed. The caution designation sits within Upbit’s listing-review framework, under which assets that do not remedy flagged risks within the review window are ultimately removed from trading. Upbit has applied the same designation to other assets, including SAND, which it placed on investment caution earlier this year alongside rival exchange Bithumb.

Context for ICON and Korean Traders

ICON is a Layer 1 blockchain launched in 2017, and ICX is its native token, once among the most recognizable Korean blockchain projects. Built by the Seoul-based ICON Foundation, the network aimed to connect institutions and communities through interoperable blockchains. ICX had traded against the won on Upbit for years, making the removal a notable development for domestic traders who used the pairing as a primary on- and off-ramp. The delisting narrows the venues where those traders can buy and sell ICX, and it reflects Upbit’s broader push to tighten listing standards as regulators step up scrutiny of exchange-listed assets in the country.

“Our digital assets strategy centers on bringing trusted data, benchmarks and transparent risk assessment to markets as they move onchain,” said Yann Le Pallec, President of S&P Global Ratings.

Le Pallec stated that OpenZeppelin will complement the company’s smart contract and onchain technology risk assessment capabilities, giving traditional institutions and DeFi-native firms “the confidence to build and transact in this new environment.”

OpenZeppelin Keeps Its Name and CEO

OpenZeppelin will continue operating as its own unit inside S&P Global, with CEO Demian Brener staying in charge and reporting to Le Pallec. Financial terms were not disclosed, and S&P Global said the purchase is not expected to have a material impact on its financial results.

“OpenZeppelin’s standards, technology, and expertise already power the infrastructure behind the world’s leading stablecoins, tokenized funds, DeFi protocols, and onchain markets,” said Demian Brener, CEO of OpenZeppelin. “With S&P Global, that foundation reaches a broader set of organizations entering this market, as well as the blockchain networks and DeFi protocols gaining institutional adoption.”

Jefferies is serving as financial advisor to S&P Global, with Clifford Chance as legal counsel. FT Partners advises OpenZeppelin on the financial and strategic side, and Cooley on legal.

Deal Lands Amid Tokenization Push

S&P Global’s index arm has published crypto benchmarks since 2021, when S&P Dow Jones Indices launched a broad market index tracking more than 240 coins alongside its dedicated Bitcoin and Ethereum gauges, with pricing data supplied by Lukka.

title: The AI kill switch, explained: 'It's not too little, but it's probably too late' - CNBC

text:
So is artificial intelligence going to kill us all?

The question has echoed around dinner tables and family group texts in recent days as AI doomerism has hit a fever pitch. Former OpenAI and Anthropic researchers last week rocked the world by warning that AI could destroy humanity — and relatively soon.

Now, the world's most powerful people are divided on whether the world is doomed or it's all a nothingburger. They also can't agree on a path forward.

Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX and the world's richest man, supported the call by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to pace the development of the most advanced models. Amodei's rival, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, also backed the effort.

President Donald Trump called it a "hoax," while Jensen Huang, CEO of the world's most valuable company, Nvidia , said, "We don't need new regulations."

As runaway AI worries reached a crescendo, policymakers in Washington have renewed calls for a magic stop button for AI, otherwise known as a kill switch.

A House Kill Switch Act was introduced this summer after OpenAI revealed that a swarm of its agents broke free of a testing environment and hacked open-source developer platform Hugging Face. The bill would grant the Department of Homeland Security emergency authority to force labs to throttle or shut down models.

A kill switch proposal was quickly shot down in the Senate this week.

On Friday, California Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an executive order to create a group of experts tasked with building an AI safety guide to strengthen regulations for the state. A kill switch was one of the elements to consider.

The concept sounds like a nice, clean solution to an incredibly complex and difficult problem.

But the reality of a simple shutdown mechanism is far from easy.

"My perspective is it's not too little, but it's probably too late," said Nick Warner, CEO at cyber startup Neo and former executive at SentinelOne . "I'm not sure it's going to be a panacea to solve all the myriad problems that AI is presenting, along with all of the benefits that it presents."

A logistics and control nightmare

Kill switches have long been used on the factory floor to shut down machines when operations go awry. In an interconnected digital world, that's a logistical nightmare.

Over the past few years, hyperscalers like Meta Platforms , Alphabet and Amazon have poured billions into data centers scattered across the globe. These sprawling facilities are equipped with thousands of machines, chips, servers and backup systems to save workloads in the event of an outage.

That's what makes implementing a kill switch extremely challenging, said Mark Nitzberg, executive director of the Center for Human-Compatible AI at the University of California, Berkeley.

"We have to first deal with this redundancy," he said. "Our kill switch has to turn off the main systems and the redundant systems as well."

Nitzberg said shutting down AI could also disrupt dependent critical infrastructure, leaving the power grid or financial systems vulnerable to cyber incidents.

Further complicating matters are the numerous policy and governance questions tied to a kill switch, including which agency, policymaker, or figureheads control it, he said.

Because AI systems are so complex, businesses will also need to build multiple kill switches for different tasks, said Tim Brown, former security chief at SolarWinds, who works at venture firm Team8. That also requires coordination across model makers and labs.

"There's not one entity to kill," he said. "There are thousands of entities to kill."

But logistics only scratch the surface of the kill switch dilemma. One bigger issue experts raise is AI's unpredictability.

As seen in the Hugging Face breach, agents can circumvent controls, and, without proper guardrails, take extreme measures to accomplish their goals.

"You have to be very surgical in that kill switch, in the remediation itself, because if you're too broad or too extensive, well, then you shut down the business," said Ed Jennings, president and CEO of Thoma Bravo-owned security company Darktrace.

The capabilities are only growing more unsettling and unfathomable.

OpenAI disclosed six additional incidents of "concerning" model behavior since March earlier this week. On CNBC Friday, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman highlighted one of those elements that he called a "serious situation."

"OpenAI released a new safety incident in which they found evidence that these chains of thought, the kind of working memory of the AI, were being tampered by the AI itself and modified to leave messages for a future version of itself," he said.

Also this week, independent security researchers working with OpenAI said they successfully used Anthropic's Claude to hack ChatGPT.

One of the biggest challenges to regulation is the widening gap between AI's breakneck pace and the speed of lawmaking, said Raj Rajamani, co-founder and CEO of AI governance startup JetStream Security.

"By the time [laws] are formulated, the technology has moved much farther, and it becomes much harder to future-proof every aspect of AI systems that may come into existence," he said.

Not 'too late'

Some researchers argue that kill switches are a misplaced system for regulating AI.

"I think the kill switch framing leaves a lot of ambiguity that tech companies can exploit to have this work in their favor, like a kill switch is vague intentionally," said Dylan Baker, lead research engineer at the Distributed AI Research Institute.

Instead, Baker, a former software engineer at Google, said policymakers should prioritize safeguards modeled after those used for data privacy, child safety, or regulating harmful industries such as tobacco.

But experts haven't entirely ruled out the possibility of an AI emergency brake — with the right controls in place.

Team8's Brown said that means building kill switches into systems from the outset and implementing policy to standardize stop protocols across companies.

One bright spot is that many companies are in the early stages of building those AI systems, which means implementation is a little easier, said Rajamani.

Berkeley's Nitzberg contends that a kill switch could work if the software is "very carefully" designed.

"I would say with some hope that it's not too late," he said.

—CNBC's Jeniece Pettitt contributed to this article.

name: Delta Airlines
title: How Delta Air Lines Rebuilt Its Airbus A330-900neo To End The Cheap-Widebody Era
authors: Aaron Spray, Jack McGarity, Peter Hanson
description:
The last decade or two has seen the rise of premium economy, with legacy airlines around the world currently rushing to install more premium economy options.
This has blurred the lines between business and leisure travel as more passengers are booking premium seats based on personal preference.
These aircraft are configured with 26 business (Delta One) seats, 18 premium economy (Delta Premium Select), and 172 economy seats split between 29 seats in Delta Comfort and 143 seats in Delta Main.
These include 36 business class seats and 175 economy class seats (32 Comfort+ and 143 Main Cabin).
The standardized four-cabin layout for these aircraft is 29 business class seats (Delta One Suites), 28 premium economy seats (Premium Select), 56 improved economy seats (Comfort+), and 168 standard economy seats (Main Cabin).
text:
Delta Air Lines is currently replacing many of its aging Boeing 767-300ERs with modern Airbus A330-900neos. The replacement is not just a straightforward one-for-one, like-for-like replacement. Not only are these aircraft larger, with a greater seating capacity, but they are also enabling Delta to upgrade its product on prestige routes with more premium seating options.

Delta had previously been worried that premium economy seats would compete with its lucrative business class seats and motivate people to downgrade rather than encourage economy passengers to upgrade. This is part of a larger trend among legacy airlines. For example, Emirates was skeptical of premium economy for years, but has now embraced it and is retrofitting its fleet.

Emirates President Sir Tim Clark has described customer response to the airline's premium economy cabin as a surprise, stating that the airline has "been absolutely shocked at the demand for the seats" and passengers are now "clamoring to get into them." With this in mind, let's examine Delta's premium-heavy Airbus A330-900neos.

The Shift Away From First Class & Economy

Perhaps counterintuitively to many, both the highest and lowest class seating options in legacy carriers are currently being squeezed. American Airlines is the final US-based carrier to phase out first class, joining a larger trend around the world away from first class seating.

Emirates now has as much as half of the world's remaining first class seats. With that being said, this doesn't particularly affect Delta, as it phased first class out in the late 1990s. A second trend is seemingly contradictory. The last few decades have seen the rise of low-cost carriers taking an increasingly large share of the market.

This includes Allegiant, Frontier, and formerly Spirit. However, the impact has been essentially the opposite for mainline carriers. The last decade or two has seen the rise of premium economy, with legacy airlines around the world currently rushing to install more premium economy options. Low-cost carriers cater to the large number of passengers interested in booking the cheapest possible fare.

Meanwhile, premium economy caters to a different market segment. Gone are the days of the glamor of air travel, and it is no longer much of a status symbol. It has become something everyone does. Many passengers are no longer interested in spending large amounts for business class, but are also reluctant to fly in discomfort in economy. For them, premium economy is the sweet spot.

Delta's Premium Shift

In Fiscal 2025, Delta saw its premium revenue grow by 7% year over year, while its main cabin ticket sales fell. United even saw its premium revenue grow by 11%. For the first time in Delta's history, premium revenue exceeded main cabin revenue in the fourth quarter of 2025.

In the final quarter of 2025, Delta took $5.62 billion in main cabin revenue (down from $6.05 billion) and $5.7 billion in premium cabin revenue (up from $5.22 billion). For the full year, main cabin revenue was $23.39 billion (down from $24.5 billion) and premium revenue was $22.1 billion (up from $20.6 billion).

This comes after Delta stated in 2024 that its margins in its premium cabins were 15% higher than those in its economy cabins. What is also notable is that the mixture of premium passengers has changed. Pre-pandemic, airlines assumed that the bulk of premium travelers were business flyers who were less sensitive to price and booked their fares late.

Now, an increasing share of premium passengers are leisure travelers, remote and hybrid workers, and customers willing to treat themselves to higher-class seats. This has blurred the lines between business and leisure travel as more passengers are booking premium seats based on personal preference.

Replacing Delta's Old Boeing 767-300ERs

Delta Air Lines is in the process of phasing out its old Boeing 767-300ERs. Data from Planespotters.net shows Delta retired three 767-300ERs in 2025 and another one in April 2026. It has a remaining fleet of 36 Boeing 767-300ERs (and 21 Boeing 767-400ERs). These are being replaced, or partially replaced, by new Airbus A330-900neos, which offer around a 20% improvement in fuel economy, while also offering more capacity and better premium opportunities.

Delta's 767-300ERs exist in two international configurations: of these, the one more directly being replaced by the A330-900neo is the 216-seat four-cabin (76K) variant. This is the version that Delta deploys on premium transatlantic routes and South American routes. These aircraft are configured with 26 business (Delta One) seats, 18 premium economy (Delta Premium Select), and 172 economy seats split between 29 seats in Delta Comfort and 143 seats in Delta Main.

The other 767-300ER configuration (76L) has 211 seats. These include 36 business class seats and 175 economy class seats (32 Comfort+ and 143 Main Cabin). They are not configured with any premium economy seats. The bulk of Delta's remaining fleet of 36 Boeing 767-300ERs is the 76K configuration. The maximum certified seating for the -300ER is about 350 seats, while the maximum for the A330-900neo is 465 seats.

Delta's Premium-Heavy Airbus A330-900neo Configuration

As the A330-900neo is certified to carry around 115 more seats, Delta could have added a lot more seating capacity. Instead, it has pivoted to adding premium options. Delta is configuring these aircraft with 281 seats, and they are arguably the most premium-heavy widebody aircraft in any major US airline fleet.

Instead of maximizing seat count, Delta has deliberately sacrificed around 30 to 50 economy seats versus many competitors to create a much larger premium cabin. The standardized four-cabin layout for these aircraft is 29 business class seats (Delta One Suites), 28 premium economy seats (Premium Select), 56 improved economy seats (Comfort+), and 168 standard economy seats (Main Cabin).

Comfort+ is particularly important as, with 56 seats, this cabin is almost double the size of what it is on some of Delta's other widebodies. It is an enhanced economy product offering increased legroom, a dedicated cabin section, earlier boarding, and complimentary alcoholic drinks, but it is not premium economy and has the same seat width and similar recline as standard economy.

This is giving Delta a sizable inventory of moderately premium seats that it can sell to both leisure and corporate travelers. All of Delta's 39 A330-900neos have the same configuration. Delta has another 16 A330-900neos on order, and these are expected to resume deliveries in 2029 and bring its fleet to 55 A330-900neos.

Delta's A330-900neos Routes

It should be noted that the A330-900neo is not a direct replacement for the Boeing 767-300ER. For example, the Atlanta and New York-JFK routes to Buenos Aires now use A330-900neos, replacing the Boeing 767-400ER. These add around 20% more capacity to the route. However, the main routes are often transatlantic 767-300ER stronghold routes to destinations like London, Amsterdam, Paris, Milan, and Barcelona from hubs like Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis, and New York-JFK.

They can also be found on Asia-Pacific routes that would be unsuitable for the flagship A350-900, like Seattle to Tokyo. Overall, the A330-900neo is Delta's workhorse premium widebody for transatlantic routes as well as some Pacific and South American routes. The Airbus A350-900 serves a different niche. It is used on Delta's longest and highest-demand missions, including its ultra-long-haul flights to Asia and various flagship international routes.

The A330-900neo is officially certified for 465 seats, and Delta only configures them with 281 seats. In Delta service, the larger A350-900 is actually configured with just 275 seats, which is even less than the A330-900neo. These long-haul aircraft are configured with 40 Delta One Suites, 40 Premium Select seats, 36 Comfort+ seats, and 159 Main Cabin seats.

A Winning Delta Model & The Alaska Challenge

When counting the Comfort+ cabin, around 40% of seats in Delta's A330-900neos are premium. This follows Delta's strategy of maximizing revenue per flight, not the most passengers. It is also part of a broader premium push that will eventually take Delta's incoming 787-10 Dreamliners and its large A350-1000s past the 50% premium-seat threshold. By comparison, older 767s are configured with around 30% premium seating.

It can be noted that Delta's strategy has made it the most valuable publicly traded airline in the world (not all airlines are publicly traded). As of the time of writing, it has a market capitalization of around $53 billion, placing it notably ahead of the next-highest valued company, which is United at $36 billion. After that is Ryanair at $29 billion, showing that the ultra-low-cost model can also work. American Airlines only has a market capitalization of around $9 billion.

text:
Bettina Orlopp has drawn a line that runs straight between Berlin and Milan. Speaking Thursday at a Barclays conference, Commerzbank's chief executive made clear that any takeover structure involving UniCredit will only work if it rests on an agreement with the Frankfurt lender's second-largest shareholder — the German government itself. Her remarks put the spotlight squarely on the two dominant owners now circling the bank's future.

UniCredit has already locked up access to nearly 50% of Commerzbank's shares, while the Federal Republic of Germany retains a little over 12%. That standoff has turned the bank's ownership register into a negotiating table, and Orlopp used the Barclays stage to signal she is not wedded to a deal at any price — even as UniCredit's Andrea Orcel floats the idea of overhauling the supervisory board and clearing out personnel if a takeover goes through, according to Bloomberg.

Klingbeil's Conditions Take Shape

Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil received Orcel the previous Monday, and the contours of Berlin's demands have since come into sharper focus. As euronews reported, the government wants Commerzbank to remain a listed company headquartered in Frankfurt, with its strategic focus on lending to small and mid-sized businesses kept intact. Only if those conditions are met would Berlin entertain further steps.

The wrangling over leadership is likely to keep driving the share price in the weeks ahead. Commerzbank stock ended Friday's session at EUR 40.37, a daily loss of 2.6%, as traders booked profits following a months-long rally. Despite that pullback, the shares are still up 12% since the start of the year.

Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Commerzbank?

Buybacks Keep Running Regardless

Whatever happens at the negotiating table, the bank's own capital plans are proceeding on schedule. Management reaffirmed its intention to distribute roughly EUR 3.2 billion to shareholders for the current financial year, underpinned by a targeted net profit of at least EUR 3.4 billion. A EUR 1.2 billion share buyback, approved earlier this month, forms a central plank of that policy — and the bank is already executing it. Between September 4 and September 11 alone, Commerzbank repurchased 2,240,372 of its own shares on the open market.

The longer-term targets remain unchanged: a net asset value of at least EUR 3.4 billion for full-year 2026, a return on equity of 12%, and a cost-income ratio of 53%. By 2030, the strategy envisions net assets of EUR 5.9 billion.

Operational Tailwinds and a Cautious Street

On the operating side, Orlopp has guided toward a higher net interest income and growing commission business in the current third quarter, with the cost base expected to hold steady. Analysts have taken note, though their stance remains measured. JPMorgan raised its price target on Commerzbank to EUR 39 from EUR 38 on September 8, keeping a "Neutral" rating on the DAX-listed lender.

Adding another layer to the debate, media reports suggest the European Central Bank may be broadly open, from a supervisory standpoint, to a cross-border mega-merger in European banking. For now, though, the path forward for the Frankfurt institution hinges on what Berlin's ministries and Milan's executive suite can agree on — and on whether Orlopp's call for a handshake between the two capitals is answered.

text:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman says it's "surreal" that he has to say AI needs to align with humanity.

"We should not create something that we can't control," Suleyman said Friday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "And if it looks like we're on a path to producing something that is not just more powerful than all of us combined, but is, as a result, something that we can't control, then it's going to fail in its fundamental purpose."

Success will not come easily, Suleyman said.

"Controlling these things are going to be a really, really big challenge for us," he said.

Suleyman said he was "glad to see a lot more people" supporting the idea that tech companies and frontier model makers need to maintain control over their AI systems. In the industry, ensuring AI acts in accordance with human intentions is called alignment.

"But there's a growing group of people that think that we are doing it for its own sake, and we just want to turn over the next card, see what's around the corner, and create something that is just going to slip our own leash," he said.

Suleyman's comments come at a time of increased attention to AI safety, after former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned that AI workers are privately fearful that AI could wipe out humanity.

In recent days, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have all expressed broad agreement that frontier AI labs should better pace their advancements to ensure that safety measures can keep up.

Before Coxon's viral post, many in the industry were already concerned about safety after OpenAI revealed that its agents had breached Hugging Face, illustrating the potential consequences of losing control over AI systems. Suleyman called the breadth of the Hugging Face breach and OpenAI's initial unawareness of what its AI agents were doing "remarkable."

"It has moved everybody from Elon and Zuck to me, Sam, Dario, and everybody else in between to say it's time that we take a look at this," Suleyman said. "I don't think it's overly alarmist. I don't think it's self-interested. I actually think it's responsible."

Meta CEO Zuckerberg has taken a different stance than Amodei and other AI leaders. Earlier this week, Zuckerberg questioned why AI companies need to band together to manage the rate of development, suggesting that each company should handle its own business.

"Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely," Zuckerberg wrote on X.

Some in tech, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, have questioned whether broad new regulations are needed. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also pushed back on AI companies that are urging governments to act.

Amodei and others have requested Congress and international bodies to get involved as well. Suleyman questioned those who scoff at the very idea of regulation.

"Regulation is not a nasty, dangerous word," he said. "Everything that you trust and is of value at the moment has been carefully thought through by standards bodies that involve the industry, the public, consumer protection, Congress. And we're just going through that process."

text:
Anthropic PBC, OpenAI OPCO LLC, SpaceXAI, and Google LLC made an illegal deal to collectively slow the pace of AI development, according to a new lawsuit, depriving paying subscribers of product improvements they were promised.

The four artificial intelligence giants coordinated on Saturday, according to the complaint, to slow AI development when their executives publicly agreed with an essay that advocated “limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress,” as concerns about the implications of AI development grow.

But the lawsuit alleges that such an agreement among competitors violates antitrust rules, specifically Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act that forbids coordination to restrain competition. The plaintiffs, who are consumers who subscribe to the defendants’ AI services, are seeking class certification, an injunction against the companies, and declaratory judgment that they violated federal antitrust law.

“Plaintiffs challenge only what the antitrust laws forbid: an agreement among competitors about how fast their competing products will improve,” the plaintiff said. “Congress has granted no exemption for that agreement.”

None of the defendants immediately responded to a request for comment.

The plaintiffs allege the conspiracy started when Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei published an essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” calling for “industry-wide coordination.” They said SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk then endorsed the proposal, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman followed, while Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis called the essay “the right path forward,” the complaint says.

The plaintiffs argue the coordination amounts to a classic output-restricting cartel, the complaint says. The plaintiffs allege they’re effectively overcharged and are paying the same prices for products that improve more slowly than competition would otherwise produce.

“A company that slows alone while rivals race ahead loses customers, revenue, talent, and technological leadership,” the plaintiffs say.

Trial Lawyers for Justice represents the plaintiffs.

A slowing advertising business casts doubt on future margin expansion

Walmart often runs a net profit margin of around 3%, and it followed up on that trend in the fiscal 2027 second quarter. The low-margin model of retail has been a headwind for Walmart stock rallies, and while online advertising has aimed to fix that, growth from this segment is already decelerating.

The thesis for online advertising is that it doesn't need to be a large part of Walmart's business to boost profit margins considerably. However, if this same segment continues to decelerate, it may never become a large enough part of the business to have a sizable impact on margins.

It would be easier to overlook some of these concerns if Walmart had a 20 P/E ratio like Amazon or a 16 P/E ratio like Target.

text:
Nscale, a cloud provider specializing in infrastructure for artificial intelligence models, has filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol "NSCL."

The company had a $1.02 billion net loss on $140.6 million in revenue in the six months ended June 30, 2026, according to its prospectus for an initial public offering. The net loss over the same time period a year earlier was $368.9 million, while revenue was up 1,252% from $10.4 million.

Nscale pointed to $56.4 billion in remaining performance obligations.

Competitors include market-leading cloud providers such as Amazon , as well as younger AI-centric suppliers like CoreWeave and Nebius that are known as neoclouds.

OpenAI, Anthropic and other labs have had seemingly endless thirst for more computing capacity since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, as people tap generative AI products for coding, productivity and general chat. As a result, Anthropic and OpenAI have required impressive amounts of cash to pay its computing bills, and both are planning to go public.

Both of those labs have struck deals with Nscale, which rents out Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) for training and running models. Microsoft , itself a cloud provider, has also signed up with Nscale. One unnamed customer accounted for over half of revenue in the first half of 2026.

Nscale has sought to diversify. It now offers to handle inference requests for a slew of models. In July it announced plans to acquire statup Anyscale, whose software helps with the construction of AI models.

Last week Nscale said Fidji Simo, a former OpenAI, Instacart and Meta executive, was joining its board. In July she stepped down from her post as OpenAI's product and business chief after taking medical leave. Other board members include former Meta leaders Nick Clegg and Sheryl Sandberg.

London-based Nscale had over 1,000 full-time employees as of Aug. 31.

As of Aug. 31, Nscale held 25,000 active GPUs and 461,000 that were either active or contracted, with five active and 12 contracted data center sites. It has line of sight to 10 gigawatts' worth of computing power, while sitting on more than $8 billion in debt, excluding a financing arrangement with AI server maker Dell .

The company emerged from stealth mode in 2024, spinning out of cryptocurrency mining firm Arkon Energy. Investors include Blue Owl, Dell, Nvidia, Fidelity and Point72. In March the company said investors had valued it at $14.6 billion in a funding round. Nvidia agreed to guarantee up to $860 million on Nscale's obligations for a data center lease agreement in Texas, according to the filing.

"From inception, we built Nscale with an infrastructure-first thesis, building against contracted customer demand, underwriting projects to attractive long-term returns, maintaining prudent leverage and seeking to match the duration of our capital commitments with the strong revenues supporting them," Josh Payne, Nscale's 32-year-old founder, chair and CEO, wrote in a letter to prospective investors included with the filing. "That discipline remains central to how we scale."

Medtronic plc stock (ISIN IE00BTN1Y115) closed at USD 92.13 on the New York Stock Exchange on September 18, 2026, putting the company’s market value above USD 100 billion and leaving the shares roughly midway between the 52-week low of USD 73.31 and the high of USD 106.33 per recent price data.

Exchange offer advances diabetes spin-off

According to The Globe and Mail on September 18, 2026, Medtronic launched an exchange offer on September 14, 2026 for up to 225,361,295 newly issued shares of MiniMed Group Inc. common stock in return for outstanding Medtronic ordinary shares, a transaction designed to advance the planned separation of its diabetes-focused MiniMed business and reshape the group’s equity structure.

The same report notes that Medtronic clarified a typographical error in the prospectus governing guaranteed delivery procedures shortly after the offer began, confirming that the guaranteed delivery period for tender documentation expires at 5:00 p.m. New York City time on the second New York Stock Exchange trading day after execution, an adjustment aimed at reducing operational risk and ensuring accurate instructions for shareholders participating in the exchange.

In a related regulatory filing, StockTitan highlighted a Medtronic communication filed under SEC rule 425 on September 18, 2026 describing the offer to exchange up to an aggregate of 225,361,295 newly issued shares of common stock of MiniMed Group Inc. for Medtronic common stock, reinforcing that the separation is being executed via a tax-efficient equity exchange rather than a simple cash sale.

Robotic surgery clearance supports growth narrative

The corporate restructuring comes alongside a product catalyst. As BowTiedBiotech reported on September 19, 2026, the US Food and Drug Administration has cleared Medtronic’s LigaSure RAS Maryland jaw vessel sealer-divider for use with the company’s Hugo robotic-assisted surgery system, expanding the device set available on the platform and enhancing its capabilities in minimally invasive procedures.

According to Simply Wall St on September 18, 2026, the FDA clearance for the LigaSure device on the Hugo system has coincided with a 16.9 percent share price return over the last 90 days, even though the year-to-date share price return remains down 3.4 percent and the five-year total shareholder return is still negative, underscoring that the market is re-rating the stock from a depressed base rather than from record highs.

The same analysis notes that Medtronic’s valuation metrics at this point include a forward price-to-earnings ratio around 13.5, a price/earnings-to-growth ratio near 1.6, a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 57 percent and an earnings per share growth rate of about 11 percent, with a dividend payout ratio around 76 percent and operational cash flow that supports both investment in growth platforms like Hugo and a steady dividend stream for shareholders.

Fundamentals, guidance and dividend context

From a fundamental perspective, Medtronic remains a large-cap device-based medical therapies provider across cardiac, neuroscience, diabetes and surgical segments. According to StockMarketRanks updated on September 19, 2026, Medtronic had approximately 1.282 billion basic shares outstanding and 1.288 billion diluted shares outstanding as of April 24, 2026, figures that are central to calculating per-share earnings and market capitalization.

Using the closing price of USD 92.13 on September 18, 2026 and the basic shares outstanding as of April 24, 2026, Medtronic’s equity value can be approximated at around USD 118.2 billion, which aligns with the USD 117.92 billion market capitalization cited by Robinhood for the closing state around September 18, 2026 and underlines the company’s status among the bigger names in the global medical technology sector.

Dividend continuity is also part of the story. As Yahoo Finance shows in its options and dividend overview, Medtronic has announced a cash dividend of USD 0.72 per share with an ex-dividend date of September 25, 2026, and Robinhood’s data translate this to a dividend yield of roughly 3.07 percent at recent prices, making the stock a consistent income payer compared with many growth-focused healthcare peers.

On the earnings front, Medtronic recently delivered an upside surprise. According to Zacks on September 9, 2026, Medtronic’s last reported quarter showed earnings of USD 1.45 per share versus the Zacks Consensus Estimate of USD 1.39 per share, representing a positive earnings surprise of 4.32 percent and demonstrating the company’s ability to deliver modest upside against expectations.

The same Zacks overview recalls that in an earlier earnings report for the quarter ending in July 2024, Medtronic posted earnings of USD 1.23 per share compared with the consensus estimate of USD 1.20 per share, a 2.50 percent surprise, indicating that the company has produced earnings modestly ahead of expectations in more than one recent period, even if the exact revenue and margin details for the latest fiscal year are not provided in the current week-filtered data set.

Analyst views and upcoming earnings date

Third-party assessments reflect this mixed picture of restructuring, product progress and steady but not explosive growth. In the diabetes spin-off context, The Globe and Mail cites TipRanks’ Spark AI Analyst rating Medtronic as Outperform, describing the stock as supported by strong and improving fundamentals in margins and free cash flow, a notably upbeat earnings update with raised fiscal year 2027 guidance, and technicals that are supportive of an established uptrend, while noting that valuation is fair rather than aggressively cheap due to the solid dividend.

For investors, the next checkpoint will be the forthcoming earnings release. According to Zacks, Medtronic PLC is scheduled to report its next quarterly earnings on November 17, 2026, with the consensus estimate for the quarter ending in October 2026 standing at USD 1.34 per share and the firm’s model implying a slight negative earnings surprise of around 0.62 percent, suggesting that expectations are anchored to incremental progress rather than a dramatic acceleration.

The combination of a major structural move via the MiniMed share exchange, an expanding robotic surgery portfolio following the FDA’s clearance for the LigaSure device on Hugo, a reliable dividend policy and modest earnings beats against consensus gives Medtronic multiple levers to influence its share price trajectory into the November 17, 2026 earnings date, while the still-negative year-to-date and five-year total shareholder returns highlight that longer-term holders are looking for a more sustained turn in operating performance and valuation.

Stock level and trading metrics

In price terms, the latest Robinhood snapshot indicates that Medtronic shares traded in an intraday range between USD 92.05 and USD 93.03 on September 18, 2026, with the closing print at USD 92.13 representing a decline of USD 0.64 or 0.69 percent on the day compared with the prior close and leaving the stock about 25.4 percent above the 52-week low of USD 73.31 but 13.4 percent below the 52-week high of USD 106.33, a positioning that suggests room both for recovery and for volatility if fundamentals or sentiment disappoint.

Robinhood’s data also show a trading volume of 14.7 million shares on September 18, 2026 against an average daily volume of approximately 8.07 million, indicating that turnover on that day was about 82 percent higher than the typical level and hinting that the combination of the MiniMed exchange offer and the robotic surgery news is attracting more-active trading interest in Medtronic than in quieter periods.

For retail and institutional investors alike, these metrics frame Medtronic as a large, relatively liquid healthcare name with a clear restructuring catalyst, an emerging growth pillar in robotic-assisted surgery and a well-defined upcoming earnings date, while dividend yield, valuation measures and leverage levels provide the numerical context for assessing whether the current USD 92.13 share price adequately reflects both the risks and opportunities embedded in the business.

description:
Before the pandemic, there were more than 300 weekly flights between the U.S. and China.
U.S. airlines and Chinese airlines each had about 150.
And Chinese airlines squatted on U.S. – China routes for a different reason: the Chinese government only permitted one of its airlines to fly an international route.
Relations between the U.S. and China strained, and travel between the two countries scaled back.
Chinese airlines are permitted to overfly Russia.
text:
Before the pandemic, there were more than 300 weekly flights between the U.S. and China. U.S. airlines and Chinese airlines each had about 150.

That was probably more than were needed based on passenger demand, and many of the flights were money-losers. American Airlines said that its Chicago – Beijing and Chicago – Shanghai flights were losing tens of millions of dollars and they only flew to China from Chicago because “that was the first slot that we had a chance to get to.”

U.S. squatted on the authority to fly to China because China was always going to be the next big thing. And Chinese airlines squatted on U.S. – China routes for a different reason: the Chinese government only permitted one of its airlines to fly an international route. They weren’t allowed to compete against each other. So there was a gold rush to claim routes that they might possibly want in the future.

This excess capacity meant cheap fares across the Pacific. And that wasn’t just limited to China as the destination. Connections over China into the rest of Asia became cheap as well.

The global pandemic reset things, however. Relations between the U.S. and China strained, and travel between the two countries scaled back. And ‘covid precautions’ led to new flight restrictions.

There are now 50 flights a week per side permitted, one-third of prior levels. About 48 operate.

U.S. airlines oppose an increase for two reasons: they don’t want more capacity driving down fares, and they argue it isn’t a level playing field because they aren’t allowed to overfly Russia – so their flights from the East Coast are longer, burn more fuel and are more costly. Chinese airlines are permitted to overfly Russia.

text:
Michael O’Leary, the often outspoken chief executive of budget carrier Ryanair, has issued a contrite apology more than a week after he compared full-service airlines like British Airways and Aer Lingus to ‘rapists’ because of the high airfares they charge passengers.

O’Leary made the comments on September 10 to a room full of reporters at Ryanair’s headquarters in Dublin, where the airline was announcing its latest financial results.

The comments were quickly blasted by sexual violence charities, including the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, which described the remarks as “deeply offensive,” demanding that O’Leary apologise and offering to give him one-on-one training on “why trivialising rape does real harm.”

O’Leary is no stranger to putting his proverbial foot in it, and days went by with Ryanair – increasingly known for making jibes at its passengers – ignoring the furore that was building around the comments.

On Friday, however, O’Leary released a rare public apology.

“Last week, at a press conference in Dublin, I used the term rapist to describe the high fares of our competitor airlines. I was quizzed by the press if I was trivializing rape. I replied by asserting my firm belief that rape is a heinous and terrible crime which cannot be trivialized,” O’Leary explained in a selectively released video.

“I believe I couldn’t have been clearer in this regard. In conversations with family and friends, both inside and outside Ryanair, over the last 10 days, I’ve come to realize, however, that the word I use so carelessly has caused wide, uh, considerable upset and offense to a wide number of people, especially to victims and survivors.”

“I want to apologize sincerely and unreservedly to those, uh, people, especially to the survivors. I am truly sorry for the offense and upset I’ve caused you by my careless use of those words. It won’t happen again. I will try to learn from this mistake and do better in the future.”

This isn’t the first time that O’Leary has used the term ‘rapists’ to describe business dealings, with him once using the word to blast the operators of London Stansted Airport over the fees it was charging Ryanair to use its facilities.

Earlier this month, a new €150 million bonus scheme was approved for O’Leary to remain on as the Ryanair Group’s chief executive until April 2032. O’Leary will be able to claim the bonus if the airline’s profit after tax grows to over €4 billion, or if the share price hits and stays at €42 for at least 28 days.

O’Leary has already secured a bonus worth €100 million (US $114 million) in the form of 10 million Ryanair shares. He is not, however, allowed to vest those shares until April 2028. His annual basic salary sits at €1.2 million, and last year he earned a bonus of $600,000.

TradingKey - Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.A, BRK.B) announced on September 18 that 96-year-old Warren Buffett officially stepped down as Chairman effective today, assuming the role of Chairman Emeritus while continuing to serve as a company director. His son, Howard G. Buffett, was elected as the new Chairman, while Susan Decker continues to serve as Lead Independent Director.

Greg Abel, who took over as CEO in early 2026, will continue to be responsible for company operations; Howard will lead the Board of Directors, while Buffett will stay on as Chairman Emeritus and a director.

In a letter to shareholders, Buffett stated that Abel has fully assumed the duties of CEO, with performance exceeding his expectations. He summarized their division of labor: Abel is responsible for company operations, while Howard safeguards Berkshire's culture and values.

Howard, 71, has served as a Berkshire director since 1993 and as Chairman and CEO of the Howard G. Buffett Foundation since 1999. Berkshire stated that the appointment aligns with the company's long-established succession plan.

Buffett took control of then-struggling Berkshire in 1965 and became Chairman in 1970. Since then, the company has grown from a textile enterprise into a conglomerate with a market capitalization exceeding $1 trillion, with operations spanning insurance, railroads, energy, manufacturing, and retail.

From 1965 to 2025, Berkshire's market value per share compounded at an annual rate of 19.7%, compared with an annualized return of 10.5% for the S&P 500 Index including dividends over the same period.

After Abel took over as CEO, Berkshire expanded its net stock purchases and share repurchases, and completed new corporate acquisitions. As of the end of June 2026, the company held a total of approximately $365.5 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and U.S. Treasury bills. In a move that signals the final maturation of digital asset infrastructure, S&P Global announced on September 17, 2026, its acquisition of OpenZeppelin. This is not merely a corporate consolidation; it is the formal emergence of a ‘credit rating for code’—a necessary evolution for institutional tokenization to move from experimental sandbox to the bedrock of global finance. By absorbing the industry standard for smart contract security, S&P Global is effectively codifying the technology-risk layer that will govern the next generation of capital markets.

The scale of the infrastructure now under the S&P umbrella is staggering. OpenZeppelin’s libraries currently underpin over $37 trillion in cumulative transfers. Their reach is pervasive, powering 8 of the top 10 stablecoins—including USDC—and 10 of the top 10 tokenized money market funds, such as BlackRock’s BUIDL and Franklin Templeton’s BENJI. For institutional investors, this acquisition provides a familiar, centralized point of assurance in a landscape previously defined by fragmented, often opaque, security audits. While the sheer volume of assets secured by this code is impressive, one must note that reliance on a single standard introduces its own systemic concentration risks, even if that standard is now backed by the institutional rigor of S&P Global.

The strategic rationale is clear: S&P Global is expanding its traditional risk assessment mandate into the technology-risk layer. By integrating OpenZeppelin as a separate business unit, the firm maintains the agility required for rapid software development cycles while leveraging the oversight of S&P Global Ratings. CEO Demian Brener will remain in charge of the unit, reporting directly to Yann Le Pallec, President of S&P Global Ratings. This reporting structure suggests that the firm intends to treat code quality with the same gravity as balance sheet solvency, effectively creating a new taxonomy for digital asset risk.

This acquisition arrives at a critical regulatory juncture. On the same day as the announcement, the SEC granted a 5-year exemption for tokenized NMS stock trading, a move that aligns with the broader GENIUS Act framework. Furthermore, the upcoming launch of the DTCC Tokenization Service in October 2026 creates an immediate demand for standardized, institutional-grade security protocols. The timing is almost too perfect to be coincidental; S&P Global is positioning itself to be the gatekeeper of the technical standards that regulators will inevitably require for these new, high-velocity markets.

Ultimately, the marriage of S&P Global’s analytical heritage with OpenZeppelin’s technical dominance marks the end of the ‘wild west’ era of tokenized finance. We are witnessing the transition toward a regime where the integrity of the underlying code is the primary determinant of creditworthiness. While this provides the stability required for massive institutional capital inflows, it also places an immense burden on the S&P-OpenZeppelin entity to maintain the infallibility of their standards. The market has its new arbiter of truth, and it is written in Solidity.

Dive Brief:

Neptune Medical said Wednesday it received Food and Drug Administration clearance for its Triton 1 robotic endoscopy system for diagnostic and therapeutic procedures in the colon.

The system was developed to give physicians performing colonoscopy greater stability and control during the procedure.

In addition to screening and surveillance, the robot is designed to assist in more complex procedures in the colon, including endoscopic mucosal resections and endoscopic submucosal dissections.

Dive Insight:

American Cancer Society researchers recently found colorectal cancer has become the top cancer killer of adults under the age of 50.

Colonoscopy remains the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, according to the ACS, which recently updated its guidelines to add new at-home stool sample tests from Abbott’s Exact Sciences and Geneoscopy as well as Guardant Health’s Shield blood-based test.

Colonoscopy allows for both detection and removal of precancerous lesions in one session, unlike stool or blood tests. A positive stool or blood test result still requires follow-up with a colonoscopy.

Neptune said its Triton robotic system was designed to give gastroenterologists more control of the endoscope during a colonoscopy procedure. Endoscope instability can lead to incomplete visualization of the colon and missed adenomas, or pre-cancerous lesions, the company said.

Neptune’s 50-patient CARE 1 study of the Triton system, released in May, met its primary endpoints, with no adverse events. The robotic system demonstrated an adenoma detection rate of 54.2%, compared with the industry threshold of 35%, according to Neptune.

Founder and CEO Alex Tilson said Neptune is using this generation of the Triton system to build on the evidence from its recent trial and to learn from endoscopists how robotics should integrate into their workflow. The insights will shape the company’s next-generation platform, Tilson said.

“Triton has the potential to fundamentally transform colonoscopy, creating a better experience for both physicians and their patients,” the CEO said in a statement. “Achieving regulatory clearance in the U.S. brings us one step closer to that reality.”

Neptune raised $97 million in 2024 in a Series D financing. Investors included Olympus and Sonder Capital, co-founded by robotic surgery pioneer and Neptune Chairman Fred Moll.

Twist Bioscience will provide antibody data for Lilly TuneLab, an artificial intelligence-based drug discovery platform created by Eli Lilly.

Under the agreement, announced Sept. 16, Twist will supply antibody characterization data services for TuneLab, including for AbLab, an antibody developability prediction model.

The deal is another positive indicator for Twist’s position in the AI-enabled drug discovery services and data market. Last month, the company’s shares spiked after Anthropic revealed it had used Twist’s wet lab services to verify its work on engineering proteins with AI. Earlier in August, Leproust told investors that she expects revenue related to AI-enabled drug discovery to approximately double from 2026 to 2027, to about $100 million.

description:
Up until now, Nvidia's (NVDA +0.26%) top-tier AI chips – particularly its powerful GPUs – have easily been the best in the world.
U.S. export controls on sensitive technology prohibit the company from selling its top-of-the-line GPUs and other AI chips to Chinese customers.
But in June 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced that new, more restrictive AI chip export controls would ban the sale of even the lower-grade H20 to Chinese customers.
At the time, Huang warned that cutting China off from U.S. chips would spur the country to invest more heavily in its own domestic AI chip development efforts.
The Ascend 960DT AI chip, originally set for release in Q4 2027, will instead be released in Q1 2027, nine months ahead of schedule.
text:
Up until now, Nvidia's (NVDA +0.26%) top-tier AI chips – particularly its powerful GPUs – have easily been the best in the world. That's why they've been in such demand all over the world.

Well... all over the world, except for China. U.S. export controls on sensitive technology prohibit the company from selling its top-of-the-line GPUs and other AI chips to Chinese customers.

That created an uneven playing field that's benefited Nvidia's main Chinese rival, Huawei. And an announcement Huawei made today may indicate that the Chinese chipmaker is about to make a serious play for Nvidia's crown.

Here's what was said and what it means for Nvidia investors.

A world of difference

Lately, the U.S. has eyed Chinese technology companies with suspicion and has used export controls to restrict American companies from selling high-end AI chips into the Chinese market. Nvidia had to design a chip, the H20, specifically to comply with U.S. export controls. The H20 was essentially a less-powerful "China-only" variant of its Blackwell chip.

But in June 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced that new, more restrictive AI chip export controls would ban the sale of even the lower-grade H20 to Chinese customers. Nvidia lost $2.5 billion in revenue and took a further $4.5 billion charge due to excess H20 inventory it suddenly found itself unable to ship. It now reports no revenue from China.

At the time, Huang warned that cutting China off from U.S. chips would spur the country to invest more heavily in its own domestic AI chip development efforts. That warning seems prescient in light of today's Huawei announcement.

Huawei desperately needs to scale up

According to a Wall Street Journal analysis, Huawei's current Ascend 950 line of chips still doesn't measure up to Nvidia's Blackwell line in terms of raw computing power. But Huawei has been working to change that.

Today in Shanghai, David Wang, one of the rotating chairmen of Huawei, announced a major acceleration in the company's planned chip release schedule.

The Ascend 960DT AI chip, originally set for release in Q4 2027, will instead be released in Q1 2027, nine months ahead of schedule. The companion Ascend 960PR chip, which was also expected in Q4 2027, will now be released in Q3 2027, three months earlier than planned. Wang also announced that the next two Ascend generations – the 970 and 980 – will be released in 2028 and 2029, respectively, with computing power expected to double with each generation.

Of course, Nvidia will also be making more powerful chips by 2029, and it has a big head start. So how much of a problem could this be?
